title: Three Tenses of Sense Giving
author: Nickhart
summary: This article by school leader mrnickhart introduces a temporal framework for the leadership practice of "sense giving" — the leader's role in helping a team interpret complex events and situations in ways that support collective action. Drawing on Weick's sense-making theory and Senge's iceberg model, the author distinguishes three tenses of sense giving: framing the past (retrospective, moving below surface events to explore patterns and causation), navigating the present (acknowledging ambiguity in real time while fostering trust), and inspiring the future (articulating anticipated challenges and desirable future states). Neglecting any one tense leaves a leadership gap: unattributed successes, fragmented present-day interpretation, or a reactive stance toward change. The article concludes with five narrative archetypes — origin story, overcoming the challenge, lost and found, the blind spot, and the pleasant surprise — each mapped to the tense or tenses where it is most powerful, giving school leaders a practical storytelling toolkit for sense-giving work.
points: Sense giving is not a synonym for directive communication: the relational form requires an invitation to co-construct understanding, which means leaders must embrace ambiguity rather than papering over it with false clarity.

The three-tense framework — framing the past, navigating the present, inspiring the future — maps to a different leadership competency each time, demanding different skills rather than a single 'communicate clearly' disposition.

Navigating the present is the hardest tense because it requires sense giving while the picture is still forming; done well, this vulnerability becomes a trust-building mechanism rather than a credibility risk.

The 'inspiring the future' tense extends beyond goal-setting into what the author calls Change work — architectural redesign of where judgement lives, how risk is carried, and which problems the system will stop manufacturing, not merely improvement within existing structures.

Five narrative archetypes (origin story, overcoming the challenge, lost and found, the blind spot, the pleasant surprise) provide leaders with a practical structure for combining sense giving across tenses, with each archetype assigned to the tense where its use is most natural and powerful.
quotes: The role of leadership for collective sense making is sense giving; guiding the team to interpret events and situations in a way that makes action towards educational goals more likely or more cohesive. This is not telling people what to think or presenting a narrow account of events.

Sense making is inherently retrospective; something happens and we seek to understand it: a set of academic results, patterns of pastoral incidents, fluctuating numbers on roll etc. But leaders need to look ahead, attempting predictions of future states to prepare the school for possible changes, or to paint a picture of a future desirable state.

The sense giving competency of navigating the present is challenging because it requires sense giving while the picture is still forming. But it is therefore a good opportunity to help the team to embrace ambiguity and uncertainty. It requires vulnerability but that in turn can help to develop trusting relationships.

Change work is not school improvement in the conventional sense. It is not a programme, a strategy document or an initiative. Change work is architectural. It decides where judgement lives, how risk is carried and which problems the system will stop manufacturing.

If we don't frame the past, we risk leaving successes unattributed and challenges unacknowledged, both of which are crucial to develop institutional memory. If we don't navigate the present, the team will make sense of what is happening and why from multiple, narrow viewpoints and risk fragmented decision making. If we don't inspire the future, we may remain perpetually reactive, leaving us poorly prepared for increasingly challenging times.
The beauty of narrative is that it can provide a structure for sense giving over tenses.
